25 new potential solutions per lab per year
86 new potential solutions mapped
Six potential community-led solutions identified under the climate security learning challenge:
Community led initiatives such as peace committees and resource management committees were identified as effective mechanisms in resolving resource-based conflict and enhancing social cohesion among herders and farmers
Considering that search for pasture and water drives pastoralists from the hinterland to dry season grazing areas, interventions such as the Bulto Abarufa water pan had prevented pastoralists from venturing into crop production zones thus mitigating potential conflict between herders and farmers. Water and pasture resources have an influence on pastoralist households and herd mobility. Construction of water pans needs to take into consideration this dynamic to ensure pastoralists do not migrate into farming zones in search of pasture and water.
An important endogenous resource management adaptation in terms of household mobility was the imposition of a restricted grazing area around primary schools. The protected dry season grazing zone is for the exclusive use of settled families with children in primary school. This helps prevent school going children to adopt negative drought coping mechanisms when forced to drop out of school in search of pasture for the livestock.
One of the challenges cited for low enrolment of young people in Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) institutions in Tana River County in a previous intervention was the long distance to these institutions. The pilot project afforded an opportunity to test a pop-up training centre which meant bringing trainers and training equipment to the community as opposed to trainees covering long distances to the TVET institutions. This approach saw a 100% retention rate and interest from other young people who had not been selected to participate in the motorcycle repair training.
An increasing number of pastoralists are engaging in opportunistic cultivation. While this is not new, falling herd sizes and increasing settlement among pastoralists is making it an activity with low opportunity cost for the least wealthy families. This presents an opportunity for policy intervention where the government could set up large scale reserves as dry season grazing areas.
As opposed to the older generation, young people are perceived to be optimistic in efforts that sought to enhance social cohesion. This had contributed to intermarriages for instance. There is thus an opportunity to leverage the youth dynamic in conflict mitigation especially given that young men are usually the ones who are incited to fight each other.
Eighty startups providing solutions within logistics, fintech, e-commerce, renewable energy among others were mapped during the innovation ecosystem mapping exercise. These startups have been detailed in the ecosystem mapping report. https://www.undp.org/kenya/publications/mapping-innovation-ecosystem-kenya
4 innovation methods per learning challenge
Rapid ethnography, Solutions Mapping, Co-design, Systems Thinking, Prototyping:
The climate security pilot project benefitted from the insights of an integrated approach bringing together a diverse group of stakeholders. The multiple perspectives not only helped in the design of the portfolio of experiments by taking into consideration the diverse drivers of climate related security risks but also helped surface some of the community-led solutions to climate-related security risks. Having the co-design sessions within the communities meant a better reach and practical immersion sessions with the participants. This not only helped us better understand the climate-related security risks in Tana River County but also helped us surface some of the community-led solutions. One of the challenges cited for low enrolment of young people in Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) institutions in Tana River County in a previous intervention was the long distance to these institutions. The pilot project afforded an opportunity to test a pop-up training centre which meant bringing trainers and training equipment to the community as opposed to trainees covering long distances to the TVET institutions. This approach saw a 100% retention rate and interest from other young people who had not been selected to participate in the motorcycle repair training.

Our challenge on enhancing coordination within the innovation ecosystem features several Government agencies as partners; Ministry of Information, Communications and Digital Economy, Konza Technopolis and the Kenya National Innovation Agency. The Innovation Ecosystem report was launched in December 2022 at the start of the Kenya Innovation Week by the President of Kenya and was a key piece towards shaping the Kenya Innovation Outlook and subsequent 10-year masterplan designed by the Kenya National Innovation Agency (KENIA).
The Climate Security Pilot Project involved Government agencies at the national and sub-national levels through a place-based approach.
At least one government entity or partner has adopted an Accelerator lab methods.
With Konza Technopolis, the Accelerator Lab was able to engage in sense-making to establish the value of the innovation ecosystem to innovators and harness insights to develop comprehensive research on the same.
At least 50% of our learning challenges are providing actionable knowledge to ongoing CO projects.
The Kenya Accelerator Lab was instrumental in shaping the CO CPD and the staff retreat including facilitating sessions.
Pioneered the work on digital transformation within the CO. The Accelerator Lab is part of the digital transformation task force in the country and are providing expertise and leadership in the development of a digital transformation framework. This is based upon our work with innovators and having understood and established foundational analysis and network mapping of the digital economy in Kenya.

Presented our work on disability inclusion and climate security during two weekly Global Accelerator Lab calls.
The Kenya Accelerator Lab’s work was featured and showcased in a high-level visit from the Royal Courts of Sweden and Norway to UNDP. The Accelerator lab showcased their work on engaging digital technology to support sustainable waste management and provided a platform for 10 innovators to present their work to the delegation which featured the Princess of Sweden, Prince of Norway, State Secretary of Sweden, Ambassadors and media from Sweden and Norway. This was also captured in various news outlets nationally and internationally.
The Accelerator Lab successfully organized 2 innovator showcases to provide an opportunity for local youth innovators to engage one-on-one with high-level audiences. The first was in March 2022 with the UNDP Administrator, Achim Steiner, and RBA Director, Ahunna Eziakonwa; and the second one was in November 2022, with the Crown Prince of Norway and Crown Princess of Sweden. These showcases provided a global platform for the innovators to profile their startups and mobilize pathways for further support in their scaling journeys.
The Accelerator Lab also played a key role in the formation of the UN Innovation Network in Kenya, which is an informal platform for innovation colleagues across the UN in Kenya to network, share knowledge and explore partnership on relevant interventions to harness the power of delivering as one for maximized impact.

Output 1 5 new sources of data per year - Impact of COVID-19 on MSMEs conducted with MSME Authority of Kenya - Digital inclusion webinars- 4 webinars with youth aged between 18-24 - Impact of COVID-19 on Creative Sector- Survey conducted by HEVA Fund, one of our partners. - Innovation Ecosystem mapping and analysis through the Innovation Challenges (Great COVID-19 Innovation Challenge, Disability Innovation Challenge, Creatives Innovation Challenge) - Mapping supply chain for COVID-19 PPE with Ministry of Industrialisation and UNIDO
6 different type of data sources per year - Social media analysis on COVID-19 misinformation - Geospatial data – Enabled us to get an overview of the location-based factors of informal markets in Nairobi. When mapped, we could tell that most of these markets are clustered near informal settlements. There is currently no data on all the markets and their characteristics. It was necessary to have this information to help us decide where we needed to focus our experiments informed by maximum reach. - Social media data – We looked at instances where NHIF was trending and conducted a sentiment analysis of user conversations to complement the ethnographic study. This was necessary to help NHIF understand the social sentiment of their service while monitoring online conversations. - Large scale public dialogue/FGDs – Worked with popular radio stations to broadcast interactive radio discussions on citizens’ views on NHIF. Data was then gathered through SMS questionnaires and analysed to gain rich insights into the citizens’ perceptions on provision and quality of health services. This information when triangulated with what came up during the ethnographic study, stakeholder co-creation workshop and training of champions cemented the need for practical information on the NHIF service. - Use of Innovation challenges to map grassroots solutions and uncover trends and insights on the impact of COVID-19 to the broader innovation ecosystem and how that affects minority groups like youth and PWDs - Web scrapping on the trends of work during COVID-19
35 new potential solutions per lab per year - 40 solutions mapped from the Great COVID-19 Innovation Challenge - 5 solutions mapped from the Disability Innovation Challenge - 9 solutions mapped from the Creatives innovation challenge - 5 solutions mapped through solutions safari with informal market vendors
5 innovation methods per Action Plan - Ethnography – immersions in informal markets on social protection - Positive deviance – social protection portfolio - Design thinking – prototyping with winners of Great COVID-19 innovation challenge - Gamification – addressing COVID-19 misinformation at community level - Collective intelligence – unpacking the digital inclusion challenge with diverse stakeholders - Prototyping – building and testing low-cost solutions to minimise spread of COVID-19 with local innovators from the global Hackster Detect & Protect Challenge - Co-creation – We undertook a participatory virtual stakeholder co-creation workshop with a diverse array of stakeholders that enabled people to have conversations, share perspectives and challenge each other’s thinking to arrive at an integrated understanding of the low health insurance coverage challenge and how it could be addressed. - Participatory design – By mapping stakeholders and training them as NHIF agents, we sought to build a natural network of collaborators as we thought about collective impact. We were able to see problems and opportunities from multiple perspectives. In addition, consultations with key stakeholders enabled us to identify key evidence gaps to be filled by citizen voice. - Positive deviants – The insights from the ethnographic study revealed that a good number of those who had voluntarily insured themselves had previously benefitted from the service. These were mostly those who had benefitted from the surgical package which tends to be costly. The test phase seeks to leverage the positive testimonials of these clients. - Systems thinking – From the field visits and virtual stakeholder co-creation forum, we mapped out all the factors that we needed to consider into various fields: cultural, psychological, sociological, technological, economic, demographic, biological, political and legislative. - Solutions mapping – We learnt that factors that affect design of a context specific health insurance model can come from not just technology developments, market results, media and the internet but all kinds of different sources such as internet cafes. - Ethnography – Even though the available data were useful and provided direction, they had been formulated quite narrowly. For example, “84 per cent of the Kenyan workforce is active in the informal economy” is a useful but narrow way to define the context of the informal economy in the country. In order to explore the context of the informal economy and low health insurance coverage among informal economy workers, we had to visit NHIF’s intended users, observe the way they did things, talk with them and reflect. - Data Visualization – The portfolio wheel helped us analyse the various factors and communicate our thoughts with various stakeholders during the insight validation sessions
